intro: Three questions come up again and again. Why did so many early Christians expect a thousand-year kingdom on earth, and did the apostles teach one? Is the modern state of Israel a fulfilment of prophecy, or were the promises to Israel kept long ago? And when people say “every prophecy is being fulfilled and the world is getting worse,” what does Scripture, and the record of history, actually say? This study follows the fulfilled (partial preterist) reading, sets out the evidence with timelines, maps and charts, and gives the best reply from the other side at every step.
orthodoxy: Every view in this study is held by Bible-believing Christians. The fulfilled reading here is the partial preterist one: the prophecies of Jerusalem's fall were kept in AD 70, while Christ's bodily return, the resurrection of the dead and the final judgement are still ahead, as the creeds confess. Premillennial and dispensational believers are brothers and sisters who read the same texts differently; their best arguments are given beside each answer.

parts.title: The early church and the kingdom
parts.question: Why did many early Christians expect an earthly thousand-year kingdom, and did the apostles teach it?
parts.answer: A strong line of early writers in Asia Minor and Rome expected a thousand-year reign in a rebuilt Jerusalem, drawing on Jewish hopes and a literal reading of Isaiah and Revelation 20. But the view was never universal, never written into a creed, and quite different from modern dispensationalism. The apostles themselves preached a kingdom already begun in Christ's resurrection and reign, growing until it is complete at his return.

parts.title: Israel: promises kept
parts.question: Is the founding of modern Israel an end-times event, or were the promises to Israel already kept?
parts.answer: The New Testament says the land, the seed, the throne, the temple and the new covenant were all kept in Christ, and widens the land promise to the whole world. No New Testament text predicts a return to the land. Reading 1948 as prophecy grew out of 17th-century Puritan hopes, 19th-century dispensationalism and 20th-century politics and best-sellers.

parts.title: Is the world getting worse?
parts.question: How should we answer the claim that every prophecy is being fulfilled and the world is getting worse?
parts.answer: Most of the “signs” were promised to Jesus' own generation and were fulfilled before AD 70. Every generation since has read its own news into them, and every date has failed. Meanwhile Scripture promises a growing kingdom, and the long record shows the gospel spreading and many measures of human suffering falling, even while real evil remains.

parts.title: Zionism and “replacement theology”
parts.question: Where did Zionism come from, are the claims of Christian Zionism biblical, and is the fulfilled reading “replacement theology”?
parts.answer: Zionism rose from three strands: Jewish national hopes after the pogroms of the 1880s, Protestant restorationism from the 1600s, and great-power politics. Christian Zionism reads the modern state as the keeping of God's promises. The partial preterist reading answers that the promises were kept in Christ, the true Israelite, and are shared by all who are in him, Jew and Gentile. That is not replacement but fulfilment: one olive tree, from which unbelieving branches were broken and into which they can be grafted again.

questions.q: Why did many early Christians expect a thousand-year kingdom on earth?
questions.short: They inherited Jewish hopes of an earthly messianic age, read Isaiah 65 and Revelation 20 literally, and lived under persecution that made a visible vindication on earth very attractive.
questions.answer: Early chiliasm (from the Greek for “thousand”) came from several streams at once. Jewish writings of the time, such as 4 Ezra and 2 Baruch, expected a temporary messianic kingdom before the age to come. Many believers counted the six days of creation as six thousand years of history, to be followed by a sabbath thousand-year rest. Isaiah 65 and Revelation 20 were read as a description of life on this earth. And under Roman persecution, a reign of the martyrs in the very world that had killed them was a powerful hope. The view was strongest in Asia Minor, through Papias and then Irenaeus, and in Rome through Justin and Hippolytus.
examples: Papias of Hierapolis described vines with ten thousand branches each bearing ten thousand clusters in the coming kingdom.
The Epistle of Barnabas counted the six days of creation as six thousand years, with the Son's coming bringing the seventh-day rest.
Justin Martyr expected the saints to live a thousand years in a rebuilt and enlarged Jerusalem.
questions.other: Premillennial believers see this as the plain early reading of Revelation 20, close to the apostles, which later theologians lost under the influence of allegory and of an imperial church comfortable with power.

questions.q: Did all early Christians hold this view?
questions.short: No. Justin Martyr, its best-known early defender, admitted that many Christians of “pure and pious faith” did not share it.
questions.answer: The evidence shows a real division, not a consensus. Justin, writing around AD 155, says he and others expect a thousand years in Jerusalem, but grants that many true Christians think otherwise. Many of the earliest writings say nothing at all about a thousand years: Clement of Rome, the Didache, Ignatius and Polycarp's letter all speak of Christ's return, resurrection and judgement without an earthly interim kingdom. In Rome, Gaius opposed chiliasm around 200; in Alexandria, Clement, Origen and Dionysius rejected it. The map below shows both groups across the first four centuries.
examples: Justin, Dialogue with Trypho 80: many who belong to the pure and godly faith do not hold this opinion.
Polycarp, a disciple of the apostle John, wrote of the resurrection and judgement but nothing of a thousand-year reign.
Dionysius of Alexandria persuaded a group of chiliast churches in Egypt to change their view after three days of public discussion.
questions.other: Premillennial historians reply that silence is not denial, and that the chiliasts are the earliest writers who discuss Revelation 20 at all, so they are the best witnesses to its first reading.

questions.q: Was early chiliasm the same as modern dispensational premillennialism?
questions.short: No. The early chiliasts had no pre-tribulation rapture, no separate plan for Israel, and taught that the church is the true Israel.
questions.answer: The early chiliasts expected the church to suffer under the Antichrist, then Christ to come once, raise the righteous and reign with them. Justin and Irenaeus both taught that Christians are the true Israel and the heirs of Abraham. Modern dispensationalism, shaped by John Nelson Darby in the 1830s, adds a secret rapture before a seven-year tribulation and two separate peoples of God with two programs. So a modern dispensationalist cannot simply claim the early chiliasts as forerunners; on the central question of Israel and the church, the early writers stand with the fulfilled and covenantal readings. The comparison table on this page sets the differences side by side.
examples: Justin, Dialogue 11: we who were led to God through Christ are the true spiritual Israel.
Irenaeus, Against Heresies 5.25-30: the church will face the Antichrist before the Lord comes.
No early writer teaches a rapture seven years before the return.
questions.other: Historic premillennialists agree with this and hold the early form, without a pre-tribulation rapture. Dispensationalists answer that the early church held the core truth, a future earthly kingdom, and that its details were refined as doctrine developed.

questions.q: Why did belief in an earthly thousand-year kingdom fade?
questions.short: Its critics argued from Scripture that the kingdom is spiritual and present, and its most extreme forms, with sensual feasting or a New Jerusalem in Phrygia, discredited it.
questions.answer: Several things worked together. The heretic Cerinthus and the Montanist prophets, who expected the New Jerusalem to come down at Pepuza, attached chiliasm to errors. Writers like Origen pointed out that Jesus said the resurrected neither marry nor are given in marriage, and that the kingdom is righteousness, peace and joy in the Spirit. Tyconius and then Augustine read Revelation 20 as the present reign of Christ and his saints between his two comings. It is often said the change came because the church gained power under Constantine; there is some truth in that, but Origen and Dionysius had argued the point long before Constantine.
examples: Eusebius says Papias misunderstood apostolic stories and took figurative words literally.
Augustine, City of God 20.7, says he once held a spiritual form of chiliasm before reading the thousand years as the church age.
Jerome rewrote the end of Victorinus' Revelation commentary to remove its chiliasm.
questions.other: Premillennial believers see the decline as a loss caused by allegorical reading and a church at ease with the empire, and note that chiliasm revived among Bible readers after the Reformation.

questions.q: Do the creeds say anything about a thousand-year kingdom?
questions.short: No creed teaches it. The Nicene Creed says of Christ, “his kingdom will have no end.”
questions.answer: The Apostles' Creed confesses that Christ ascended, sits at the right hand of the Father, and will come to judge the living and the dead. The Nicene Creed, in its 381 form, adds that his kingdom will have no end, written against the idea that Christ's reign would one day stop. None of the ecumenical creeds mentions an earthly interim kingdom. The churches agreed on the return, the resurrection and the judgement, and left the millennium as a matter of interpretation.
examples: Apostles' Creed: he ascended into heaven and sits at the right hand of God the Father almighty.
Nicene Creed (381): his kingdom will have no end.
The Augsburg Confession (1530), article 17, rejects the idea that the godly will rule the world before the resurrection.
questions.other: Premillennial believers point out that the creeds also do not condemn their view, and that “no end” can mean an earthly reign that flows into the eternal kingdom.

questions.q: Did the apostles expect a future earthly kingdom for Israel?
questions.short: Before Pentecost they did (Acts 1:6). After it, they preached that Christ already reigns on David's throne and that the kingdom grows through the gospel to the nations.
questions.answer: The disciples' question, “Lord, will you at this time restore the kingdom to Israel?”, shows the hope they grew up with. Jesus did not answer with a date; he promised the Spirit and sent them to the ends of the earth. Ten days later Peter announced that God had kept his oath to David by raising Christ to sit on his throne. James said the rebuilding of David's fallen tent was happening as Gentiles turned to God. Paul preached the kingdom for two years in Rome and told the Colossians they had already been transferred into it. The apostles did look forward to Christ's return and the final kingdom, but they never describe a future political reign from Jerusalem.
examples: Acts 2:30-36: David foresaw the Christ seated on his throne, and God has made him Lord and Christ.
Acts 15:14-17: the rebuilding of David's tent is fulfilled as Gentiles are called by God's name.
Colossians 1:13: he has transferred us to the kingdom of his beloved Son.
questions.other: Dispensationalists answer that Jesus did not deny a future restoration in Acts 1:7 but only declined to give its time, and that Acts 3:19-21 still looks forward to the restoration of all things at his return.

questions.q: What does Jesus' answer in Acts 1:6-8 tell us?
questions.short: He corrected the scope and the means: the kingdom would come by the Spirit, through witnesses, reaching from Jerusalem to the ends of the earth.
questions.answer: The disciples asked about the time (“at this time”), the place (“to Israel”) and the agent (“will you restore”). Jesus answered each one. The time belongs to the Father. The power would come on them by the Spirit, not by a political act. The reach would be Jerusalem, Judea, Samaria and the ends of the earth. The book of Acts follows exactly that map. So the restoration of Israel begins as Jews in Jerusalem believe, and widens as the nations are brought in.
examples: Acts 2:41: three thousand Jews believe in Jerusalem.
Acts 8:5-12: Philip preaches the kingdom in Samaria.
Acts 13:47: Paul quotes Isaiah 49:6, a light for the nations to the end of the earth.
questions.other: Dispensationalists read the answer as a postponement: the national kingdom is still promised, but the church age comes first.

questions.q: If the kingdom is already here, why do the apostles also speak of inheriting it later?
questions.short: Because the kingdom is begun now and completed at Christ's return. The reign has started; the final inheritance, in resurrected bodies, is still ahead.
questions.answer: Paul says Christ must reign until all his enemies are under his feet, the last being death, and then hand the kingdom to the Father. That means the reign is now, and its finish is at the resurrection. So believers are in the kingdom now (Colossians 1:13; Revelation 1:9) and will inherit it fully when flesh and blood are changed (1 Corinthians 15:50-54). Theologians call this “already and not yet.” What the apostles do not describe is a third stage between these two: an earthly political kingdom after the return but before the eternal state.
examples: 1 Corinthians 15:24-26: he reigns until the last enemy, death, is destroyed.
Revelation 1:9: John is a partner in the tribulation and the kingdom.
2 Peter 1:11: an entrance into the eternal kingdom.
questions.other: Premillennial believers place the thousand years between the return and the end in 1 Corinthians 15:23-24 (“then comes the end”), finding room there for an interim kingdom.

questions.q: If the apostles taught a present kingdom, why did some of their disciples' disciples expect a future earthly one?
questions.short: The line from John to Papias to Irenaeus passed on stories as well as Scripture, and the earliest sources already disagreed about how to read them.
questions.answer: Irenaeus says Papias heard John, and Irenaeus heard Polycarp. That chain is real, but it carried oral tradition, and Eusebius, who had Papias' books, judged that Papias had misread apostolic accounts and taken pictures literally. Polycarp's own letter, from the same chain, says nothing of a thousand years. Other lines from the apostles, in Rome, Antioch and Alexandria, show no chiliasm. Closeness in time is valuable, but the New Testament itself is closer still, and the second century also produced errors that no one now accepts.
examples: Irenaeus attributes the vine saying to “the elders who saw John”; no Gospel contains it.
Eusebius, Church History 3.39: Papias took things spoken in figures literally.
Second-century teachers also produced Gnostic and Montanist ideas, so early does not always mean apostolic.
questions.other: Premillennial believers see the John-Papias-Irenaeus line as strong evidence that the beloved disciple himself taught a future earthly reign, since he wrote Revelation 20.

questions.q: Was the land promise to Abraham ever kept?
questions.short: Yes. Joshua and Nehemiah both say every word of it was kept, and the New Testament widens it to the whole world.
questions.answer: Joshua says the LORD gave Israel all the land he swore to their fathers, and not one of his good promises failed. Under Solomon, Israel ruled from the Euphrates to the border of Egypt, the very limits of Genesis 15. Nehemiah, praying after the exile, says God kept his promise to give the land to Abraham's descendants, because he is righteous. The land could be lost through unfaithfulness, as the covenant warned. In the New Testament, Abraham is “heir of the world,” the meek inherit the earth, and the patriarchs were looking for a better, heavenly country. The land was a down payment on the renewed creation.
examples: Joshua 21:43-45: not one word of all the good promises failed.
1 Kings 4:21: Solomon ruled from the Euphrates to the border of Egypt.
Romans 4:13: the promise was that Abraham would be heir of the world.
questions.other: Dispensationalists answer that the promise was “forever” (Genesis 17:8), so temporary possession cannot be its full keeping, and that God must still give the land to Abraham's physical descendants.

questions.q: What does it mean that all God's promises are “yes” in Christ?
questions.short: Paul says every promise of God finds its yes in Jesus. The promises to Israel are not cancelled; they are kept, in him, for all who belong to him.
questions.answer: The promises to Israel were given to Abraham and his seed. Paul says the seed is Christ, and that all who belong to Christ, Jew or Gentile, are Abraham's seed and heirs. So the promises are not taken from Israel and given to someone else; they are kept in Israel's Messiah and shared with every believer. Jewish believers are the first heirs, and Gentiles are grafted into the same tree. The map of promises on this page shows each one beside the place where the New Testament says it was kept.
examples: 2 Corinthians 1:20: all the promises of God find their yes in him.
Galatians 3:16, 29: the seed is Christ; if you are Christ's, you are Abraham's seed.
Ephesians 2:12-19: Gentiles once strangers to the covenants of promise are now fellow citizens.
questions.other: Dispensationalists agree the promises are kept in Christ, but hold that some of them, the national and land promises, will be kept to ethnic Israel in a future kingdom.

questions.q: Must a temple be rebuilt in Jerusalem for prophecy to be fulfilled?
questions.short: The New Testament applies the temple promises to Christ and his people. Paul quotes Ezekiel's promise of God's sanctuary among his people and says, “we are the temple of the living God.”
questions.answer: Jesus spoke of his body as the temple. Paul calls the church God's temple, built on the apostles and prophets with Christ as cornerstone, and in 2 Corinthians 6:16 he quotes Ezekiel 37:27, the promise of God's dwelling among his people, as kept in the church. Hebrews says the old covenant with its sacrifices was ready to vanish, and Revelation's new Jerusalem has no temple, for the Lord and the Lamb are its temple. Ezekiel's vision of a great temple (chapters 40-48) is read in this light: a vision of God's restored presence, with a river of life that John sees flowing in the new Jerusalem.
examples: John 2:19-21: he was speaking of the temple of his body.
2 Corinthians 6:16: we are the temple of the living God, as God said (Ezekiel 37:27).
Revelation 21:22: I saw no temple in the city, for its temple is the Lord God and the Lamb.
questions.other: Dispensationalists expect a rebuilt temple, partly from 2 Thessalonians 2:4 and Ezekiel 40-48, with sacrifices as memorials; fulfilled readers place 2 Thessalonians 2 in the years before AD 70, when the temple still stood.

questions.q: Doesn't Romans 11 promise a future for Israel?
questions.short: It promises salvation for Israel through faith in Christ, not a return to the land or a state. Christians who hold the fulfilled reading differ on whether that means a large future turning of Jews to Christ.
questions.answer: Paul says God has not rejected his people: he himself is an Israelite, and there is a remnant chosen by grace. The natural branches can be grafted back in if they do not continue in unbelief, and “in this way all Israel will be saved.” Some read “all Israel” as the whole people of God, Jew and Gentile; others as the full number of the Jewish remnant through history; others, including many postmillennial writers, as a great future conversion of Jews. None of these readings needs a land or a political state: the passage is about being grafted into Christ by faith.
examples: Romans 11:5: at the present time there is a remnant chosen by grace.
Romans 11:23: they will be grafted in, if they do not continue in unbelief.
Puritans and many postmillennial writers expected a mass conversion of Jews that would bless the whole world.
questions.other: Dispensationalists read Romans 11:25-27 as the national salvation of Israel at Christ's return, tied to the restoration of the nation in its land.

questions.q: Why is the founding of Israel in 1948 not an end-times prophecy being fulfilled?
questions.short: No New Testament text predicts a return to the land, the Old Testament returns were kept after the Babylonian exile, and the covenant tied return to repentance, which a largely secular movement did not claim.
questions.answer: The prophets promised a return from exile after seventy years, and Ezra and Nehemiah record it. When later texts are claimed for 1948, such as Isaiah 11:11 or Ezekiel 37, their own context points to the return from Assyria and Babylon, and the New Testament applies their Spirit-and-covenant promises to Christ's people. Moses tied the return to Israel turning to the LORD with all its heart (Deuteronomy 30:1-3). The founding of the state was a remarkable historical event, the work of a mostly secular national movement with British and United Nations support. Christians can value it and care for its people without making it a prophetic clock.
examples: Jeremiah 29:10 and Daniel 9:2: seventy years, then return; Ezra 1:1-3 records it.
Herzl's Zionism (1896) was a secular national movement, not a religious revival.
The fig-tree reading (1948 + 40 years = 1988) failed, as did dates built on 1967.
questions.other: Dispensationalists see 1948 as God's providence keeping his word: Ezekiel 36:24-27 and 37 describe a return in unbelief followed by cleansing, and the survival of the Jewish people and their return after nearly 1,900 years is to them a sign that cannot be explained by chance.

questions.q: Is the fig tree in Matthew 24:32 a symbol of the nation of Israel?
questions.short: No. Jesus uses it as a picture of seasons, and Luke adds “and all the trees.” When the signs appear, the destruction is near, and it came within that generation.
questions.answer: Jesus says: from the fig tree learn its lesson; when its branch becomes tender and puts out leaves, summer is near. So also, when you see all these things, know that he is near, at the very gates. Truly, this generation will not pass away until all these things take place. Luke's version reads “look at the fig tree and all the trees.” The point is timing, not national rebirth. The 1970s reading that made the fig tree 1948 Israel led to the prediction that the end would come by 1988, which did not happen.
examples: Luke 21:29: look at the fig tree, and all the trees.
Matthew 24:34: this generation will not pass away until all these things take place.
The Late Great Planet Earth (1970) linked the fig tree to 1948 and a forty-year generation.
questions.other: Some dispensationalists still read the fig tree as Israel, noting Jesus cursed a fig tree as a sign against the nation (Mark 11), but most now avoid setting a length for the generation.

questions.q: Did Jerusalem's recapture in 1967 end “the times of the Gentiles”?
questions.short: Luke 21:24 is about the Roman siege and its aftermath: Jerusalem surrounded by armies, its people killed or taken captive, and the city trampled. That happened in AD 70.
questions.answer: Luke 21:20-24 begins, “when you see Jerusalem surrounded by armies, then know that its desolation has come near,” and tells the disciples to flee to the mountains. Josephus records about 97,000 captives and the city's destruction. The “trampling” of the city by the nations is the same language Revelation 11:2 uses for the holy city in that period. Jesus did not say the city would one day return to a Jewish state as a prophetic marker; he said its desolation was coming. Reading 1967 into the verse makes it say something it does not.
examples: Luke 21:20: when you see Jerusalem surrounded by armies.
Josephus, Jewish War 6.9.3: about 97,000 taken captive.
Revelation 11:2: they will trample the holy city for forty-two months.
questions.other: Dispensationalists read “until the times of the Gentiles are fulfilled” as implying a later Jewish recovery of the city, which they see beginning in 1967.

questions.q: Doesn't Genesis 12:3 mean Christians must support the modern state?
questions.short: The blessing is on Abraham and his seed, whom Paul identifies as Christ and those in him. Christians should love and bless Jewish people, but the verse is not a political instruction for a modern state.
questions.answer: God told Abram, “I will bless those who bless you, and him who dishonours you I will curse, and in you all the families of the earth shall be blessed.” Peter applies the final line to the sending of Jesus (Acts 3:25-26), and Paul says it preached the gospel in advance (Galatians 3:8). The popular link with modern foreign policy came largely through the notes of the Scofield Reference Bible (1909). Christians have every reason to love Jewish neighbours, oppose antisemitism, and pray for peace for Jews and Arabs alike, including Arab Christians in the land, without treating a modern government as beyond criticism.
examples: Acts 3:25-26: God sent his servant to bless you, as he said to Abraham.
Galatians 3:8-9: those of faith are blessed along with Abraham.
There are Arab and Palestinian Christian churches in the land today whose members are also Abraham's seed in Christ.
questions.other: Christian Zionists hold that God's blessing on Abraham's physical descendants continues, and that supporting Israel is part of honouring that promise.

questions.q: How did the founding of modern Israel come to be read as prophecy?
questions.short: Step by step: Puritan hopes of Jewish conversion and return, Darby's two-peoples theology, British restorationist politics, the Scofield Bible, and then 1948 and 1967 interpreted through best-selling prophecy books.
questions.answer: In the 1600s some English Puritans began to expect the Jews' conversion and return. In the 1830s John Nelson Darby taught that Israel and the church are two peoples with separate destinies, with a secret rapture of the church. British evangelicals such as Lord Shaftesbury urged the restoration of the Jews, and the American William Blackstone petitioned his president in 1891. The Scofield Reference Bible spread Darby's system to millions. Herzl's secular Zionism, the Balfour Declaration and the 1948 declaration of independence then seemed to confirm the scheme, and books like The Late Great Planet Earth and the Left Behind series made it popular culture. The timeline on this page traces each step.
examples: Henry Finch's book of 1621 on the Jews' restoration offended King James I.
The Blackstone Memorial (1891) asked the US president to give Palestine back to the Jews.
The Scofield Reference Bible's note on Genesis 12:3 tied the blessing to the Jewish nation.
questions.other: Christian Zionists see this history as Christians rediscovering God's faithfulness to Israel after centuries of church contempt for the Jews, and point out that some of the same Puritans were moved by love for Jewish people.

questions.q: Isn't the fulfilled reading just “replacement theology”?
questions.short: No. The church does not replace Israel; it is Israel's Messiah's own people, the one olive tree into which Gentiles are grafted. Jews are not shut out; they are welcomed back by faith.
questions.answer: “Replacement” suggests God dropped one people and picked another. The New Testament picture is of fulfilment and growth: Jesus chose twelve Jewish apostles as the core of a renewed Israel, the first church was entirely Jewish, and Gentiles were grafted into the existing olive tree. Paul calls the believing community “the Israel of God” and says the true circumcision are those who worship by the Spirit. Fulfilled readers also reject any contempt for Jewish people; the history of Christian antisemitism is a grave sin, and Paul's heart was to see his own people saved.
examples: Romans 11:17: you, a wild olive shoot, were grafted in among the others.
Galatians 6:16: peace and mercy be upon the Israel of God.
Romans 10:1: my heart's desire and prayer to God for them is that they may be saved.
questions.other: Critics reply that whatever it is called, the view still transfers Israel's national promises to the church, and that the term “Israel” in Paul nearly always means ethnic Israel.

questions.q: Aren't the signs of Matthew 24 being fulfilled today?
questions.short: Jesus gave the signs to his disciples about their own generation, and history records them before AD 70. Every generation since has found the same signs in its news.
questions.answer: The disciples asked when the temple would be destroyed. Jesus spoke of false christs, wars, famines, earthquakes, persecution, the gospel preached to the nations, and the abomination of desolation, and then said this generation would not pass away until all these things took place. Acts and Josephus record false prophets, the famine under Claudius, earthquakes, persecution and the Roman armies around Jerusalem, all within forty years. Wars and earthquakes have happened in every century since, so finding them in today's news proves nothing about today. The study on Matthew 24 goes through every verse.
examples: Acts 11:28: Agabus foretold a great famine, which took place in the days of Claudius.
Colossians 1:23: the gospel has been proclaimed in all creation under heaven.
Josephus records false prophets leading crowds into the desert before AD 70.
questions.other: Futurist readers hold that the signs are “birth pains” that grow in frequency and intensity before the return, so their recurrence today still matters.

questions.q: Doesn't “as in the days of Noah” mean the world will get more and more wicked?
questions.short: Jesus' point in Matthew 24:37-39 is that people were unaware: eating, drinking and marrying until the flood came. It is about suddenness, not a rising graph of evil.
questions.answer: Genesis does describe great wickedness before the flood, but Jesus draws a different lesson. He lists ordinary things, eating, drinking, marrying, and says they did not know until the flood came and swept them away. The warning is to be ready because the judgement comes suddenly to people going about normal life. Those “taken” in the comparison are taken by the flood, in judgement. Nothing in the passage says the world must grow steadily worse before Christ comes.
examples: Matthew 24:38-39: eating and drinking, marrying and giving in marriage, and they were unaware.
Luke 17:28-30 adds the days of Lot: buying, selling, planting, building.
Matthew 24:42: stay awake, for you do not know on what day your Lord is coming.
questions.other: Many futurists still read the comparison as including the moral state of Noah's world (Genesis 6:5, 11), and see growing violence and corruption as part of the sign.

questions.q: What about 2 Timothy 3: “in the last days there will come times of difficulty”?
questions.short: Paul tells Timothy to avoid such people. The “last days” had already come, and Paul adds that the deceivers “will not get very far.”
questions.answer: Paul lists lovers of self, lovers of money, the proud and the abusive, and then says, “avoid such people.” That only makes sense if they were in Timothy's world. The New Testament says the last days began with Christ: God has spoken in these last days by his Son, and Peter called Pentecost the last days of Joel. Verse 9 says the false teachers will not get very far, for their folly will be plain to all. Verse 13 says evil people and impostors go from bad to worse, deceiving and being deceived: that describes the impostors, not the whole world.
examples: 2 Timothy 3:5: avoid such people.
Hebrews 1:2: in these last days he has spoken to us by his Son.
2 Timothy 3:9: they will not get very far.
questions.other: Futurist readers agree the last days began at Pentecost, but say they end in a final period when these sins reach a peak.

questions.q: Does Luke 18:8, “will he find faith on earth?”, mean faith will nearly die out?
questions.short: The question ends a parable about praying and not losing heart. It challenges the hearers to keep believing; it is not a forecast that the church will shrink.
questions.answer: Jesus told the parable of the widow and the unjust judge to show that his disciples ought always to pray and not lose heart. God will give justice to his elect speedily. Then comes the question, “when the Son of Man comes, will he find faith on earth?” In context, it presses the hearers: will you keep praying until he vindicates you? The vindication of the persecuted disciples came within their generation. Meanwhile the number of Christians has grown from about 560 million in 1900 to well over two and a half billion.
examples: Luke 18:1: they ought always to pray and not lose heart.
Luke 18:7-8: he will give justice to them speedily.
Christians in Africa grew from about 9 million in 1900 to over 650 million by 2020.
questions.other: Some futurist readers take the question as a hint of widespread unbelief at the very end; others agree it is a challenge rather than a forecast.

questions.q: Isn't the great falling away of 2 Thessalonians 2 happening now?
questions.short: Paul told the Thessalonians the mystery of lawlessness was “already at work” and that they knew what was restraining it. The falling away came in their generation.
questions.answer: Paul wrote to calm believers who thought the day of the Lord had come. First, he said, the rebellion must come and the man of lawlessness be revealed. He reminded them he had told them these things, said they knew what was holding him back, and said the mystery of lawlessness was already at work. Jesus had warned that many would fall away before the end of that age, and the later letters record it: all in Asia turned away from Paul, and John wrote that many antichrists had already come and gone out from the church.
examples: 2 Thessalonians 2:5-7: you know what is restraining him; the mystery of lawlessness is already at work.
2 Timothy 1:15: all who are in Asia turned away from me.
1 John 2:18-19: many antichrists have come; they went out from us.
questions.other: Futurists hold that the rebellion and the man of lawlessness are still future, at the end of the age, and often see today's decline in Western churches as its approach.

questions.q: Is the world really getting worse?
questions.short: Some things are worse and much is better. On long-run measures, extreme poverty, child deaths and illiteracy have fallen sharply, and the church has grown more in the last century than in any before.
questions.answer: News reports what goes wrong, and each generation remembers the past as calmer than it was. The long record tells a more mixed story. Around 1800 about four in ten children died before age five; today it is under four in a hundred. Life expectancy has more than doubled. Extreme poverty has fallen from over a third of humanity in 1990 to under a tenth. Real evils remain, and some are new. The Christian claim is not that progress is automatic, but that the risen Christ is ruling, and his kingdom, like yeast, keeps working through the whole loaf.
examples: Child deaths before age five: about 43% around 1800, about 4% today.
Life expectancy: about 29 years in 1800, about 73 today.
Christians worldwide: about 0.56 billion in 1900, about 2.6 billion today.
questions.other: Premillennial believers answer that material progress is not spiritual progress, that secular Western culture is declining fast, and that Scripture expects evil to ripen before the end.

questions.q: How has the church grown since the apostles?
questions.short: From about 120 believers in Acts 1 to around 2.6 billion people who call themselves Christians, with the fastest growth in the last century in Africa, Asia and Latin America.
questions.answer: Acts begins with about 120 disciples. By 300 the church may have numbered several million in the Roman Empire. In 1900 about 558 million people were Christians, most of them in Europe and North America. By 2025 the figure is about 2.6 billion, and the centre has shifted to the global South: Africa alone went from about 9 million Christians in 1900 to over 650 million. That is what the parables of the mustard seed and the leaven describe: small beginnings, great growth.
examples: Acts 1:15: about 120 believers.
Acts 2:41; 4:4: three thousand, then five thousand.
Africa: about 9 million Christians in 1900, over 650 million in 2020.
questions.other: Some reply that counting nominal Christians overstates true faith, and that numbers do not measure the health of the church.

questions.q: Are earthquakes increasing, as is often claimed?
questions.short: No. The US Geological Survey reports roughly the same number of major earthquakes each year over the last century; we simply detect and hear about more of them.
questions.answer: The USGS notes that about fifteen earthquakes of magnitude 7 or greater happen in an average year, and that this rate has stayed fairly constant. There are many more seismograph stations now, so far more small earthquakes are recorded, and news travels instantly. Jesus did mention earthquakes in various places as the beginning of birth pains, and in that generation there were notable ones, including the earthquake at Philippi in Acts 16 and a destructive one at Laodicea around AD 60.
examples: USGS: about 15 earthquakes of magnitude 7 or more per year on average.
Acts 16:26: a great earthquake shook the prison at Philippi.
Tacitus records an earthquake that destroyed Laodicea in AD 60.
questions.other: Some futurists accept that the count is steady but say that the human impact of earthquakes, with larger cities, is greater, or that the sign is not about numbers at all.

questions.q: Are wars getting worse?
questions.short: Wars remain terrible, but deaths in battle per head of world population are far below the levels of the two world wars.
questions.answer: Research groups that count battle deaths, such as the Uppsala Conflict Data Program and the Peace Research Institute Oslo, show that the rate of battle deaths per 100,000 people fell steeply after 1945. It rose again with the wars in Ethiopia and Ukraine after 2020, but remains a small fraction of its 20th-century peak. Jesus said, “you will hear of wars and rumours of wars; see that you are not alarmed, for this must take place, but the end is not yet.” Wars were never meant as a countdown.
examples: Matthew 24:6: the end is not yet.
In the Second World War, battle deaths ran at over 100 per 100,000 people a year; in most recent years, a few.
AD 66-70 saw civil war in Rome (the year of the four emperors) and the Jewish revolt.
questions.other: Others warn that nuclear weapons make the risk of a catastrophic war greater than ever, so falling averages give false comfort.

questions.q: How do I answer a friend who says every prophecy is being fulfilled?
questions.short: Ask which prophecy and which verse, read it in context with them, look at who it was spoken to and when, and show how many generations have said the same thing.
questions.answer: Start with the text, not the news. Ask: who was this spoken to, and what did it mean to them? Look for time words such as “this generation,” “soon,” “near,” or “some standing here.” Check whether the New Testament already says it was fulfilled. Then look at history: every century has had wars, earthquakes and famines, and every generation of date-setters has been wrong. Finally, point to the promises of a growing kingdom. Do it with humility: your friend loves the Lord and wants to be ready, which is good.
examples: Matthew 16:28: some standing here will not taste death until they see the Son of Man coming in his kingdom.
Revelation 1:1, 3: things that must soon take place; the time is near.
Dates set for 1844, 1914, 1988 and 2011 all failed.
questions.other: Futurists answer that prophecies can have near and far fulfilments, so a first-century fulfilment does not rule out a greater one at the end.

questions.q: Why does it matter whether we expect the world to get better or worse?
questions.short: What we expect shapes how we live. A hope that Christ is winning gives courage to evangelise, build, serve and plan for the long term.
questions.answer: If believers expect only decline, it is easy to retreat, to see every problem as a sign, and to fear the news. Scripture gives Christians a different posture: Christ has all authority, he is with us to the end of the age, and the nations will be discipled. The apostles faced far worse than most believers do today, yet they turned the world upside down. Expecting the kingdom to grow does not mean ignoring suffering; it means working against it in Christ's name, confident that our labour in the Lord is not in vain.
examples: Matthew 28:18-20: all authority has been given to me; make disciples of all nations.
1 Corinthians 15:58: your labour is not in vain in the Lord.
Jeremiah 29:7: seek the welfare of the city where I have sent you.
questions.other: Premillennial believers have also built hospitals, schools and missions, and answer that urgency about Christ's return has itself been a great motive for evangelism.

questions.q: What does Scripture promise about the growth of Christ's kingdom?
questions.short: A stone that becomes a mountain filling the earth, a mustard seed that becomes a tree, yeast that leavens all the dough, and a government whose increase will never end.
questions.answer: Daniel saw a stone cut without hands strike the statue of the empires and become a great mountain that filled the whole earth, a kingdom set up in the days of those kings. Jesus compared the kingdom to a mustard seed and to yeast. Isaiah says of the child on David's throne, “of the increase of his government and of peace there will be no end.” The Psalms promise that all the ends of the earth will turn to the LORD. Paul says Christ must reign until all his enemies are under his feet. These are pictures of steady, unstoppable growth during this age.
examples: Daniel 2:35, 44: the stone became a great mountain and filled the whole earth.
Matthew 13:31-33: the mustard seed and the leaven.
Habakkuk 2:14: the earth will be filled with the knowledge of the glory of the LORD.
questions.other: Amillennial and premillennial believers read these as describing the kingdom's final glory at Christ's return, or its spiritual reach, rather than a visible growth within history.

questions.q: Doesn't the parable of the wheat and weeds show evil growing with good until the end?
questions.short: Yes, both grow together until the harvest; the parable does not say the weeds win. In the same chapter, the mustard seed and the leaven describe the kingdom spreading.
questions.answer: Jesus says the field is the world and both wheat and weeds grow until the harvest at the end of the age. That guards against expecting a perfect world before the end, and against trying to root out evil by force. But the parable gives no proportion; it does not say the weeds will take over the field. Matthew sets it beside the mustard seed and the yeast, so the whole chapter teaches both: evil persists, and the kingdom grows.
examples: Matthew 13:30: let both grow together until the harvest.
Matthew 13:31-32: the smallest seed becomes a tree.
Matthew 13:33: until it was all leavened.
questions.other: Premillennial readers see the parable as the main picture of this age: a mixed field that only Christ's return will put right.

questions.q: What is Zionism, and how is Christian Zionism different?
questions.short: Zionism is the movement for a Jewish national home in the land of Israel. Christian Zionism is the belief, held by some Christians, that supporting that state is a biblical duty because it keeps God's promises.
questions.answer: Political Zionism, launched by Theodor Herzl in 1896, was largely secular: a response to European antisemitism seeking a safe national home for Jews. Religious Zionism added a Jewish theological reading. Christian Zionism is older than both, rooted in 17th-century Protestant hopes of a Jewish return, and shaped in its modern form by dispensationalism. It teaches that the land promises belong to the Jewish nation today, that the state of 1948 is prophecy fulfilled, and that Christians are bound to support it. A Christian can reject Christian Zionism as a theology while loving Jewish people and supporting their safety and that of their neighbours.
examples: Herzl's The Jewish State (1896) argued from persecution, not from Scripture.
Some strictly Orthodox Jewish groups opposed Zionism, holding that only the Messiah should bring the return.
Christian Zionist organisations such as the International Christian Embassy Jerusalem (1980) and Christians United for Israel (2006) lobby on Israel's behalf.
questions.other: Christian Zionists see the return of Jews to the land after nearly two thousand years as God's hand in history, whatever the motives of the secular founders.

questions.q: Why did Zionism rise in the late 19th century?
questions.short: Because of persecution: the Russian pogroms of 1881-82 and the Dreyfus affair in France convinced many Jews that they would never be safe without a state of their own.
questions.answer: After the assassination of Tsar Alexander II in 1881, waves of violence swept Jewish communities in the Russian Empire. Leon Pinsker wrote Auto-Emancipation (1882), and the first organised settlers went to Ottoman Palestine. In Paris, the false conviction of the Jewish officer Alfred Dreyfus (1894) and the antisemitism around it moved the journalist Theodor Herzl to write The Jewish State and to call the First Zionist Congress in Basel (1897). British politicians, some raised on restorationist Bible teaching and some moved by war aims, issued the Balfour Declaration (1917). The Holocaust then made the case for a Jewish state overwhelming in many eyes.
examples: 1881-82: pogroms in the Russian Empire.
1897: First Zionist Congress, Basel.
1903: the British offer of land in East Africa was debated by the Zionist Congress and finally declined.
questions.other: Christian Zionists see God's providence even in these painful causes, as he used Pharaoh and Cyrus to move his people.

questions.q: What happened to the people already living in the land?
questions.short: In the war of 1947-49 about 700,000 Palestinian Arabs, Muslim and Christian, fled or were driven from their homes. They remember it as the Nakba, “the catastrophe.”
questions.answer: The UN partition plan of November 1947 proposed Jewish and Arab states. Fighting followed, and after Israel declared independence in May 1948, neighbouring Arab states invaded. By the end of the war about 700,000 Palestinians had become refugees, and hundreds of villages were emptied. Historians still debate how much was flight and how much expulsion. Christians must hold together compassion for Jews who had just survived the Holocaust and for Palestinians, including ancient Christian communities, who lost their homes. A theology that sees only one people in the land fails the command to love our neighbour.
examples: UN General Assembly Resolution 181 (1947): the partition plan.
Palestinian Christian families in towns like Lydda and Ramla were among those displaced.
Palestinian Christians today number in the tens of thousands in the West Bank and Gaza, and more as citizens of Israel.
questions.other: Supporters of Israel stress that Arab leaders rejected partition and began the war, and that a similar number of Jews left or were expelled from Arab countries after 1948.

questions.q: Was the land promise unconditional?
questions.short: The promise to Abraham was certain, but living in the land was always tied to covenant faithfulness. Israel was warned it would be expelled for unfaithfulness, and it was, twice.
questions.answer: God swore the land to Abraham's seed, and Joshua says he kept that oath. But Moses repeatedly made staying in the land conditional: the land would vomit Israel out as it had the Canaanites if they defiled it. The exile to Babylon and then the destruction of AD 70 are those warnings carried out. The return was promised to a people who turned back to the LORD with all their heart. The unconditional heart of the promise, a seed through whom the world is blessed and an inheritance that cannot fail, is kept in Christ and widened to the whole renewed earth.
examples: Leviticus 18:28: lest the land vomit you out when you make it unclean.
Deuteronomy 28:63-64: you shall be plucked off the land; the LORD will scatter you among all peoples.
Hebrews 11:13-16: they died not having received the things promised, seeking a better country.
questions.other: Christian Zionists separate the unconditional ownership of the land from the conditional enjoyment of it: Israel could be removed for sin but never lose its title.

questions.q: Will God curse nations that do not support Israel (Genesis 12:3)?
questions.short: The promise was to Abraham and his seed, whom Paul names as Christ and those in him. The New Testament applies it to the blessing of the gospel, not to foreign policy.
questions.answer: God promised to bless those who bless Abram and curse him who dishonours him. Peter applies the promise to the sending of Jesus (Acts 3:25-26), and Paul says it was the gospel preached beforehand (Galatians 3:8-9). The people who bless Abraham's seed are those who receive Christ. Applying the verse to a modern government's policies makes political support a test of faithfulness, which Scripture never does. Christians should certainly oppose antisemitism and seek the good of Jewish people, as of all people.
examples: Acts 3:25-26: God sent his servant to bless you by turning you from wickedness.
Galatians 3:9: those of faith are blessed along with Abraham.
The link with modern foreign policy was popularised by the Scofield Reference Bible's notes (1909).
questions.other: Christian Zionists argue that the promise also covers Abraham's physical descendants, and point to the fate of empires that persecuted Jews.

questions.q: Do Jewish people have their own covenant and not need Jesus?
questions.short: No. Peter told the leaders of Israel there is salvation in no one else, and Paul's heart's desire was for Israel to be saved through Christ.
questions.answer: Some voices within or near Christian Zionism suggest that Jews are saved through God's covenant with Israel apart from faith in Jesus, or that Christians should not share the gospel with Jews. Most evangelical Christian Zionists reject this, and rightly. The apostles preached first to Jews: the gospel is the power of God for salvation, to the Jew first and also to the Greek. Jesus himself is Israel's Messiah, and to withhold him from Jewish people is the opposite of love.
examples: Acts 4:10-12: Peter to the rulers of Israel: there is salvation in no one else.
Romans 1:16: to the Jew first.
Romans 10:1: my prayer to God for them is that they may be saved.
questions.other: Dual-covenant writers appeal to Romans 11:29, that God's gifts and calling are irrevocable, and to the history of forced conversions that make evangelism of Jews painful.

questions.q: Romans 11:29 says God's gifts and calling are irrevocable. Doesn't that prove Israel's national promises still stand?
questions.short: It proves God has not given up on Israel: he still calls Jewish people, and they can be grafted back into their own tree by faith. It says nothing about land or a state.
questions.answer: Paul's point is that God's choice of Israel has not been cancelled by their present unbelief. Because of that calling, God keeps a remnant and will graft natural branches back in if they do not continue in unbelief. The calling is to Christ, and its gift is salvation. In the same chapter Paul says branches were broken off because of unbelief and stand or fall by faith. The verse is a reason to hope and pray for Jewish people to come to Jesus, not a promise of territory.
examples: Romans 11:20: they were broken off because of their unbelief, but you stand fast through faith.
Romans 11:23-24: how much more will these be grafted back into their own olive tree.
Romans 11:1: I myself am an Israelite.
questions.other: Christian Zionists read the irrevocable calling as including the whole package of promises given to the nation, land included.

questions.q: Is the fulfilled reading “replacement theology”?
questions.short: No. Replacement means God threw Israel away and chose the church instead. Fulfilment means Israel's Messiah gathered a renewed Israel around himself, Jew first, and opened the doors to the nations.
questions.answer: The church began as a Jewish movement: Jesus chose twelve Jewish apostles, the first thousands of believers were Jews, and Gentiles were added to them. Paul does not picture two trees, or an old tree cut down and a new one planted, but one olive tree, rooted in the patriarchs, with some branches broken off and others grafted in. Jewish believers are not replaced; they are the natural branches. So the true division is not between Israel and the church, but between those in Christ and those not yet in him. The olive-tree diagram on this page shows the three models side by side.
examples: Acts 2:41: three thousand Jews were added in one day.
Ephesians 2:14-16: he made the two one, creating in himself one new man.
Romans 11:17: you were grafted in among the others.
questions.other: Critics reply that any view denying a distinct future for ethnic Israel functions as replacement, whatever its intent.

questions.q: Doesn't fulfilment theology lead to antisemitism?
questions.short: Christian antisemitism is real and shameful, but it contradicts the New Testament, written almost entirely by Jews. Fulfilment theology rightly held leads to love and prayer for Jewish people.
questions.answer: The church's history includes terrible sins against Jews: violent sermons, expulsions, forced conversions and pogroms, and some Christians drew on theology to excuse them. Those sins must be named and repented of. But the cause was pride and hatred, which Paul specifically forbids: do not be arrogant toward the branches. Paul, who taught that believers are Abraham's seed, also said he could wish himself cut off for the sake of his people. The fulfilled reading, properly held, calls Christians to the same grief and longing.
examples: Romans 11:18-20: do not be arrogant toward the branches; do not become proud, but fear.
Romans 9:1-3: great sorrow and unceasing anguish for my kinsmen.
Many churches have formally repented of their past teaching of contempt for Jews.
questions.other: Christian Zionists argue that only an ongoing role for ethnic Israel guards fully against contempt, and point to the history of Christian antisemitism as evidence.

questions.q: Does the New Testament ever call the church “Israel”?
questions.short: Yes, in substance and in words: Paul blesses “the Israel of God,” Peter gives the church Israel's titles from Exodus 19, and James writes to “the twelve tribes in the dispersion.”
questions.answer: Paul says not all who are descended from Israel belong to Israel, and that the true circumcision are those who worship by the Spirit of God. He closes Galatians with peace on all who walk by this rule, and on the Israel of God. Peter calls the scattered believers a chosen race, a royal priesthood, a holy nation, the very words God spoke to Israel at Sinai, and adds Hosea's “once you were not a people.” Gentile believers were once alienated from the commonwealth of Israel, but are now fellow citizens with the saints. Each of these joins believing Gentiles to believing Israel; none excludes Jewish people.
examples: Romans 9:6: not all who are descended from Israel belong to Israel.
1 Peter 2:9-10: a holy nation, God's own people.
Ephesians 2:12, 19: no longer strangers, but fellow citizens.
questions.other: Dispensationalists read “the Israel of God” as believing Jews only, and say Peter's titles describe the church by analogy without making it Israel.

fathers.name: John the apostle
fathers.says: Wrote Revelation 20. What he meant by the thousand years is the very question in dispute.

fathers.name: Clement of Rome
fathers.says: Speaks of Christ's coming, the resurrection and judgement, with no thousand-year kingdom.

fathers.name: The Didache
fathers.says: Ends with watchfulness, the deceiver, the resurrection and the Lord coming on the clouds; no millennium.

fathers.name: Cerinthus
fathers.says: A false teacher said to expect an earthly kingdom of bodily pleasures; his name made later writers wary of chiliasm.

fathers.name: Ignatius of Antioch
fathers.says: Stresses Christ's real death and resurrection and the end; nothing on a thousand years.

fathers.name: Papias
fathers.work: Expositions of the Sayings of the Lord (fragments)
fathers.says: Taught a bodily kingdom of a thousand years on this earth after the resurrection. Eusebius thought he misread figurative words.

fathers.name: Epistle of Barnabas
fathers.says: Six days of creation as six thousand years, then the Son's coming and a sabbath rest. Scholars debate whether that rest is on earth.

fathers.name: Polycarp
fathers.says: A disciple of John; his letter speaks of resurrection and judgement but never of a thousand years.

fathers.name: Justin Martyr
fathers.says: Expects a thousand years in a rebuilt Jerusalem, yet admits many Christians of pure faith think otherwise; calls the church the true Israel.

fathers.name: Montanist prophets
fathers.says: Expected the New Jerusalem to come down at Pepuza; their excesses discredited chiliasm in many churches.

fathers.name: Irenaeus
fathers.says: A kingdom of the righteous in the renewed creation before the final judgement; the church faces the Antichrist first.

fathers.name: Gaius of Rome
fathers.says: Opposed chiliasm and linked it with Cerinthus.

fathers.name: Clement of Alexandria
fathers.says: The rest of the saints is spiritual; no earthly thousand-year kingdom.

fathers.name: Hippolytus
fathers.says: Six thousand years of history, then the sabbath kingdom; placed the end around AD 500 to calm date-setters.

fathers.name: Tertullian
fathers.says: A thousand-year kingdom in a Jerusalem come down from heaven after the resurrection.

fathers.name: Origen
fathers.says: Criticised those who hope for eating, drinking and an earthly Jerusalem; the promises are spiritual.

fathers.name: Nepos
fathers.says: Defended an earthly thousand-year kingdom against allegorical readers.

fathers.name: Dionysius of Alexandria
fathers.says: Debated Nepos' followers for three days until they changed their minds.

fathers.name: Victorinus of Pettau
fathers.says: The first Latin commentary on Revelation; Jerome later rewrote its chiliast ending.

fathers.name: Methodius
fathers.says: A thousand-year feast of tabernacles in the resurrection, given a strongly spiritual sense.

fathers.name: Lactantius
fathers.says: Christ will reign a thousand years among the righteous, with the earth richly fruitful.

fathers.name: Eusebius
fathers.says: Preserved the record of the debate and judged Papias a man of limited understanding.

fathers.name: Tyconius
fathers.says: Read the thousand years as the church age between Christ's comings.

fathers.name: Jerome
fathers.says: Called the expectation of an earthly golden Jerusalem a fable.

fathers.name: Augustine
fathers.says: Once held a spiritual chiliasm; came to read the thousand years as Christ's present reign with his saints.

compare.modern: Israel and the church are two distinct peoples with separate programs.

compare.early: No rapture before the tribulation; the church faces the Antichrist.
compare.modern: The church is caught up before a seven-year tribulation.

compare.early: Antichrist, Christ's one return, resurrection of the righteous, thousand-year kingdom, final judgement.
compare.modern: Rapture, seven-year tribulation, return, thousand years with mortal nations and a restored national Israel, final rebellion, judgement.

compare.early: The Antichrist sits in a temple; no restored sacrificial worship for believers.
compare.modern: A rebuilt temple, often with sacrifices as memorials during the kingdom.

compare.early: Six-day creation week as six thousand years; Isaiah 65; Revelation 20; persecution.
compare.modern: A consistent literal hermeneutic; unconditional promises to ethnic Israel; a gap in Daniel's seventy weeks.

compare.early: A respected opinion that many orthodox Christians did not share; in no creed.
compare.modern: A system formed in the 1830s, spread by the Scofield Bible, conferences and popular books.

compare.early: Kept to the saints, Abraham's seed, in the renewed earth.
compare.modern: To be kept to the nation of Israel in the land of Canaan.

promises.promise: To your offspring I give this land, from the river of Egypt to the Euphrates.
promises.kept: Not one of all the good promises failed; all came to pass. Solomon ruled to the Euphrates.
promises.other: The promise is everlasting, so a future, permanent possession is still owed to Israel.

promises.promise: All the land of Canaan, for an everlasting possession.
promises.kept: Abraham's promise was to be heir of the world; the meek will inherit the earth; the fathers sought a heavenly country.
promises.other: The wider inheritance is added to the land of Canaan, not a replacement for it.

promises.promise: In your offspring shall all the nations of the earth be blessed.
promises.kept: The offspring is Christ, and all who belong to Christ are Abraham's offspring.
promises.other: Abraham also has a physical seed, Israel, with its own continuing promises.

promises.promise: In you all the families of the earth shall be blessed.
promises.kept: God sent his servant Jesus to bless you, as he promised Abraham; the gospel was preached beforehand to Abraham.
promises.other: The blessing on those who bless Abraham's descendants still applies to the nation.

promises.promise: When seventy years are completed for Babylon, I will bring you back to this place.
promises.kept: In the first year of Cyrus, the LORD stirred him to send the exiles home to rebuild.
promises.other: A second, worldwide return was still to come after the first.

promises.promise: The Lord will extend his hand a second time to recover the remnant of his people.
promises.kept: The first time was the exodus from Egypt (11:16); the second, from Assyria and Babylon. Paul applies the root of Jesse rising for the nations to the Gentile mission.
promises.other: The worldwide scope (“four corners of the earth”) points to the modern return.

promises.promise: I will open your graves, bring you into the land of Israel, and put my Spirit within you.
promises.kept: Ezekiel explains the bones as the exiles. The new-covenant Spirit of Ezekiel 36-37 is given to Christ's people, written on hearts.
promises.other: The bones came together in 1948 without breath; the Spirit will come at a future national conversion.

promises.promise: I will establish the throne of his kingdom forever.
promises.kept: God raised Christ to sit on David's throne at his right hand.
promises.other: Christ now sits on the Father's throne; David's throne will be taken on earth at the return.

promises.promise: I will raise up the booth of David that is fallen, that they may possess all the nations.
promises.kept: James says this is happening as Gentiles are called by God's name.
promises.other: James shows Gentile inclusion agrees with Amos, while the rebuilding itself waits for the kingdom.

promises.promise: I will make a new covenant with the house of Israel and Judah.
promises.kept: Jesus' blood is the new covenant; Hebrews quotes Jeremiah in full and calls the old covenant obsolete.
promises.other: The church shares the new covenant's spiritual blessings; its national promises await Israel.

promises.promise: My dwelling place shall be with them; my sanctuary in their midst forevermore.
promises.kept: Paul quotes these words and says, we are the temple of the living God.
promises.other: Ezekiel 40-48 still describes a literal future temple in the land.

promises.promise: I will pour out my Spirit on all flesh.
promises.kept: Peter: this is what was uttered through the prophet Joel.
promises.other: Pentecost was a first instalment; the cosmic signs of Joel 2:30-31 are still future.

promises.promise: They will look on me, on him whom they have pierced, and mourn.
promises.kept: John: these things took place that the Scripture might be fulfilled.
promises.other: The national mourning of Israel at Christ's return is still future (Revelation 1:7).

promises.promise: In the place where it was said, you are not my people, they shall be called children of the living God.
promises.kept: Paul applies this to the calling of Gentiles as well as Jews.
promises.other: Hosea speaks of Israel's future restoration; Paul only draws an analogy.

promises.promise: The Deliverer will come from Zion; he will banish ungodliness from Jacob.
promises.kept: Paul places this in the gospel age: a remnant chosen by grace now, Jews and Gentiles in one olive tree. Many fulfilled readers also expect a large future turning of Jews to Christ.
promises.other: Romans 11:26 is the national salvation of Israel at Christ's return.

test1948.q: Does Moses tie the return to the land to Israel turning back to the LORD?
test1948.yes: Then a return led by a largely secular national movement does not match the return Moses described.
test1948.no: Some read Ezekiel 36:24-27 as a return first and cleansing after; that is the strongest case for 1948.

test1948.q: Did the prophets' promised return from exile already happen?
test1948.yes: Then the exile promises have a recorded fulfilment, as Ezra, Nehemiah, Haggai and Zechariah say.
test1948.no: Those who say no read the return under Cyrus as partial and look for a fuller one.

test1948.q: Does any New Testament text predict a return to the land?
test1948.yes: Supporters point to Luke 21:24 and Romans 11; neither mentions a return to the land.
test1948.no: Then the apostles, who knew the prophets best, did not expect one; they widened the promise to the world.

test1948.q: Is the fig tree in Matthew 24:32 a symbol of the nation?
test1948.yes: Then “this generation” set the end by about 1988, which did not happen.
test1948.no: Luke adds “and all the trees”: it is a picture of seasons, and the generation was Jesus' own.

test1948.q: Is a modern state the same as the covenant people?
test1948.yes: Then citizenship would decide covenant standing, which Paul denies.
test1948.no: Then the promises belong to Christ and those in him, Jew and Gentile, wherever they live.

claims.claim: Wars and rumours of wars are increasing.
claims.reply: Jesus said “the end is not yet” and spoke of wars his disciples would hear about. The Jewish revolt and Rome's year of four emperors (AD 69) filled that generation.
claims.data: Battle deaths per head of world population are far below the levels of the world wars, though they rose again after 2020.
claims.other: Modern weapons make the potential for destruction greater than ever.

claims.claim: Earthquakes are getting more frequent.
claims.reply: Earthquakes “in various places” are the beginning of birth pains, not the end. There were notable earthquakes in that generation.
claims.data: The USGS reports about 15 earthquakes of magnitude 7+ a year with no significant increase over the past century.
claims.other: The sign may be about impact or awareness rather than numbers.

claims.claim: Pandemics like COVID-19 are end-time plagues.
claims.reply: Famine and plague struck that generation (Acts 11:28). Far worse pandemics came long before ours.
claims.data: The Black Death killed perhaps a third of Europe; the 1918 flu tens of millions. Each was also read as the end.
claims.other: Plagues are part of the pattern of birth pains, which some expect to intensify.

claims.claim: People are lovers of self and money as never before: these are the perilous last days.
claims.reply: Paul tells Timothy to avoid such people: they were in his day. The last days began with Christ.
claims.data: Each list in Paul's letters describes sins of every age (Romans 1:29-31).
claims.other: The last days began at Pentecost but may end with an intensified version of these sins.

claims.claim: Evil will go from bad to worse until the end.
claims.reply: Paul says impostors go from bad to worse, deceiving and deceived; but four verses earlier, “they will not get very far.”
claims.data: The verse describes deceivers, not the world as a whole.
claims.other: The pattern of deceivers worsening can apply to every age, including ours.

claims.claim: It is like the days of Noah: violence everywhere.
claims.reply: Jesus' point is unawareness: eating, drinking and marrying until the flood came.
claims.data: The passage names ordinary activities, not a rising graph of evil.
claims.other: Genesis 6 also stresses violence, so the moral state may be part of the comparison.

claims.claim: Israel's rebirth in 1948 started the final generation.
claims.reply: Luke adds “and all the trees”; the generation was Jesus' own.
claims.data: Predictions built on 1948 (1981, 1988) and 1967 all failed.
claims.other: Most dispensationalists now accept the fig tree as Israel without setting a date.

claims.claim: Technology like chips and digital money is preparing the mark of the beast.
claims.reply: Revelation was written to seven churches about things that must soon take place; the number fits Nero Caesar.
claims.data: Barcodes, credit cards, computers, RFID and vaccines have each been named as the mark.
claims.other: The mark may be literal and future, and today's technology makes it possible for the first time.

claims.claim: The great falling away is happening in today's churches.
claims.reply: Paul said the mystery of lawlessness was already at work and the readers knew what restrained it.
claims.data: 2 Timothy 1:15 and 1 John 2:18-19 record mass defections in the apostles' lifetime.
claims.other: The final apostasy is still future, at the end of the age.

claims.claim: Faith is dying out; Jesus said he might not find faith.
claims.reply: The question ends a parable telling disciples not to lose heart; it is a challenge, not a forecast.
claims.data: Christians numbered about 0.56 billion in 1900 and about 2.6 billion today.
claims.other: Nominal numbers say little about living faith.

claims.claim: Once the gospel reaches every nation, the end will come.
claims.reply: Paul says the gospel had been proclaimed in all creation under heaven and was bearing fruit in the whole world.
claims.data: Colossians 1:6, 23 and Romans 10:18 describe the gospel's reach in Paul's day.
claims.other: “All nations” means every people group, which mission agencies still count as unreached.

claims.claim: Evil and good grow together, so the world cannot get better.
claims.reply: Both grow, but the parable gives no proportion; the mustard seed and leaven in the same chapter describe growth.
claims.data: Matthew 13 holds both truths: evil persists, and the kingdom spreads.
claims.other: The mixed field is the main picture of this age until Christ returns.

results.title: A fulfilled and advancing hope
results.text: The signs were kept in AD 70, Christ reigns now, and his kingdom grows until it fills the earth before his bodily return. This is the reading followed in this study.

results.title: Postmillennial hope
results.text: Christ reigns now and the gospel will win the nations before his return, with some signs still future.

results.title: Amillennial hope
results.text: Christ reigns now; the thousand years are this age; good and evil grow together until his return.

results.title: Historic premillennial hope
results.text: Christ reigns in heaven now and will return to reign a thousand years on earth, as many early writers held, without a separate plan for Israel.

results.title: Dispensational hope
results.text: The kingdom offered to Israel was postponed; the church will be raptured, and Christ will reign from Jerusalem over a restored Israel.

zion.intro: Zionism is a word with many meanings. This part traces how it rose, sets out the strongest claims of Christian Zionism with the partial preterist reply to each, and answers the charge that this reading is “replacement theology.” It distinguishes theology from politics: rejecting Christian Zionism as a reading of Scripture is not hostility to Jewish people, and Christians are called to love Jews and Palestinians alike.

terms.meaning: The modern movement for a Jewish national home in the land of Israel, launched politically by Herzl in 1896.
The Christian belief that the modern Jewish state keeps God's promises and that supporting it is a biblical duty.
Hostility or prejudice against Jewish people. Always sinful, and rejected by every view in this study.
The idea that God rejected Israel and chose the church instead. Fulfilment theology rejects this label.
The view that God's promises to Israel are kept in Christ, the true Israelite, and shared by all in him, Jew and Gentile.
The idea that Jewish people are saved by God's covenant with Israel apart from faith in Jesus.
The older Protestant hope, from the 1600s, that the Jews would be restored to their land, often joined to a hope of their conversion.
