claims.claim: The land belongs to the Jewish people forever by an unconditional covenant.
claims.case: God alone passed between the pieces in Genesis 15, binding himself; “everlasting possession” cannot mean a temporary one.
claims.reply: God kept the oath (Joshua 21:43-45), but residence in the land was always conditional on faithfulness (Leviticus 18:28; Deuteronomy 28:63). The everlasting inheritance is the whole renewed earth, promised to Abraham's seed, Christ and those in him (Romans 4:13; Matthew 5:5).

claims.claim: Nations that bless Israel are blessed; those that oppose it are cursed.
claims.case: The promise has no expiry date and history shows persecutors of Jews falling.
claims.reply: The New Testament applies the promise to Christ and the gospel (Acts 3:25-26; Galatians 3:8-9, 16). It is not a rule for foreign policy. Christians should oppose antisemitism because every person bears God's image.

claims.claim: Isaiah 66:8 was fulfilled when Israel became a nation in a day in 1948.
claims.case: Israel was declared on a single day, 14 May 1948, as Isaiah foretold.
claims.reply: Isaiah speaks of Zion giving birth after the return from exile, with the new heavens and new earth (66:22). Paul applies Zion as mother to the Jerusalem above, mother of believers (Galatians 4:26-27). The church was born in a day at Pentecost, with three thousand added.

claims.claim: Ezekiel's dry bones came to life in 1948.
claims.case: The bones came together first without breath: a return in unbelief, then the Spirit.
claims.reply: Ezekiel explains the vision: the bones are the exiles saying “our hope is lost” (37:11). The return came under Cyrus. The promised Spirit and new heart (36:26-27; 37:14) are given in the new covenant to Christ's people (2 Corinthians 3:3).

claims.claim: Isaiah 11:11 promises a second, worldwide return, fulfilled in modern times.
claims.case: The first return was from Babylon; the second is from the four corners of the earth.
claims.reply: Isaiah counts the exodus from Egypt as the first time (11:16). The second is the return from Assyria, Egypt and the nations of his day. Paul quotes the same passage's root of Jesse rising to rule the nations as fulfilled in the Gentile mission (Romans 15:12).

claims.claim: Jerusalem must be the undivided capital of the Jewish state.
claims.case: God calls Jerusalem his city and will make it a burdensome stone to all nations.
claims.reply: The New Testament contrasts the present Jerusalem, in slavery with her children, with the Jerusalem above, which is free (Galatians 4:25-26), and tells believers they have come to the heavenly Jerusalem (Hebrews 12:22). Praying for Jerusalem's peace today means praying for all its people.

claims.claim: A third temple must be built before Christ returns.
claims.case: The man of lawlessness sits in the temple and the sacrifices must stop, so a temple must exist.
claims.reply: When Paul wrote, the temple stood, and he said the mystery of lawlessness was already at work. Daniel 9:27 was fulfilled when the sacrifices ended in AD 70. The New Testament never calls for a rebuilt temple; the church is God's temple (2 Corinthians 6:16).

claims.claim: Romans 11:26 promises the restoration of the Jewish nation in its land.
claims.case: “All Israel” in verse 26 must mean ethnic Israel, contrasted with the Gentiles in verse 25.
claims.reply: Paul speaks of salvation by grafting into Christ, never of land or a state. Readings differ on whether “all Israel” is the whole people of God, the full Jewish remnant, or a future mass conversion, but none needs a political restoration.

claims.claim: If God does not keep his promises to Israel literally, how can the church trust his promises?
claims.case: God ties Israel's continuance to the fixed order of the sun and moon.
claims.reply: God kept his promises in a greater way, as he always does: David's son reigns forever, the temple is God dwelling with his people, the land is the world. Hebrews quotes Jeremiah's new covenant as kept in Christ (Hebrews 8:8-12). Paul insists the word of God has not failed (Romans 9:6).

claims.claim: Israel's survival and military victories prove God's favour on the state.
claims.case: The odds against Israel in 1948, 1967 and 1973 were overwhelming.
claims.reply: Scripture warns against reading God's approval from success (Habakkuk 1; Luke 13:1-5). Many empires won great victories. God's favour is found in Christ, not in battlefield outcomes.

claims.claim: Ezekiel 38-39 describes Russia and Iran invading modern Israel.
claims.case: Rosh sounds like Russia, Persia is Iran, and Israel must be in the land, dwelling securely.
claims.reply: Rosh most likely means “chief” (“chief prince of Meshech and Tubal”). The nations named are ancient peoples around Israel. Revelation 20:8 uses Gog and Magog as a symbol for the nations gathered against the saints. Every generation has named a different invader.

claims.claim: The nations will be judged by how they treated the Jewish people.
claims.case: “The least of these my brothers” are Jesus' Jewish brothers.
claims.reply: In Matthew, Jesus' brothers are his disciples: whoever does the will of my Father is my brother (Matthew 12:49-50; 28:10). The judgement concerns how people treated Christ's needy followers.

claims.claim: Christians have a biblical duty to give the state of Israel political support.
claims.case: Gentiles owe a spiritual debt to the Jews and should repay it in material support.
claims.reply: Romans 15:27 is about the collection for poor Jewish believers in Jerusalem. Christians owe love to every neighbour, Jewish and Palestinian, and may judge any government's actions by God's standards of justice (Micah 6:8).

models.name: Two peoples
models.summary: Israel and the church are two peoples with two programs: earthly promises for Israel, heavenly ones for the church. This is the dispensational model behind most Christian Zionism.
models.verdict: Paul says Christ made the two one new man, breaking down the dividing wall.

models.name: Replacement
models.summary: God cut Israel off for good and planted a new, Gentile church in its place. Fulfilment theology rejects this too.
models.verdict: Paul says God has not rejected his people; he himself is an Israelite, and broken branches can be grafted back.

models.name: One olive tree
models.summary: One people of God, rooted in the patriarchs. Unbelieving branches were broken off, believing Gentiles grafted in, and Jewish people welcomed back by faith. This is the fulfilment model.
models.verdict: Paul's own picture: one tree, one root, branches in or out by faith.

olive.label: The root
olive.text: The patriarchs and God's promises to them. The root supports the branches, not the other way round.

olive.label: The trunk
olive.text: Israel's Messiah, the true seed of Abraham, in whom the promises are kept.

olive.label: Natural branches that remain
olive.text: The Jewish remnant who believed: the apostles and the first thousands. They were never replaced.

olive.label: Branches broken off
olive.text: Those of Israel who did not believe. Broken off because of unbelief, not because of their birth.

olive.label: Wild branches grafted in
olive.text: Gentile believers, sharing the root's rich sap. They must not boast.

olive.label: Grafted back in
olive.text: Jewish people who come to faith are grafted back into their own tree, more naturally than the Gentiles.

attacks.attack: Replacement theology is antisemitic and led to the Holocaust.
attacks.reply: Hatred of Jews is a grievous sin that the New Testament forbids. Fulfilment theology was taught by the Jewish apostles themselves. Nazi ideology was racial and pagan, not a reading of Romans.
attacks.distinction: Theology about the promises is not hostility to people.
attacks.rejoinder: Critics answer that centuries of church teaching of contempt prepared the ground for the Holocaust.

attacks.attack: It makes God unfaithful to his promises.
attacks.reply: Paul anticipated this charge: it is not as though the word of God has failed. All the promises are yes in Christ.
attacks.distinction: Promises kept in a greater way are not promises broken.
attacks.rejoinder: A promise of land kept by giving something else is, to critics, not the promise made.

attacks.attack: Romans 11:1 says God has not rejected his people.
attacks.reply: Agreed. Paul's proof is himself and the remnant chosen by grace. Fulfilment theology affirms Israel's continuing calling to Christ.
attacks.distinction: Not rejected means a remnant now and branches regrafted, not a separate program.
attacks.rejoinder: Dispensationalists say the remnant is the down payment on a future national restoration.

attacks.attack: The New Testament never calls the church Israel.
attacks.reply: Paul blesses the Israel of God, says not all from Israel are Israel, and calls believers the true circumcision. Peter gives the church Israel's Sinai titles.
attacks.distinction: Jewish believers are Israel's core; Gentiles are joined to them.
attacks.rejoinder: In Paul, “Israel” usually means ethnic Israel, and Galatians 6:16 may mean believing Jews.

attacks.attack: It spiritualises the plain meaning of the prophets.
attacks.reply: The apostles read the prophets this way first: James on Amos 9, Hebrews on Jeremiah 31, Paul on Hosea. Typology follows real history to its fulfilment; it is not allegory.
attacks.distinction: Following the New Testament's own reading is not allegory.
attacks.rejoinder: Dispensationalists hold that the New Testament applies these texts without cancelling their original meaning for Israel.

attacks.attack: It began with Augustine and the imperial church.
attacks.reply: Justin taught that the church is the true Israel around AD 155, long before Constantine, and the idea comes from Jesus and Paul.
attacks.distinction: Early writers on both sides of the millennium held it.
attacks.rejoinder: Critics answer that the early church's growing hostility to Judaism shaped how it read these texts.

attacks.attack: Jeremiah 31:35-37 says Israel will never cease to be a nation.
attacks.reply: The promise comes with the new covenant, which Hebrews says is kept in Christ. Israel has never ceased: its remnant lives on in Christ's people, with Jewish believers in every generation.
attacks.distinction: The continuing Israel is the believing Israel of the new covenant.
attacks.rejoinder: Critics argue “nation” must mean the ethnic people, who have survived as a people against all odds.

attacks.attack: God's gifts and calling are irrevocable.
attacks.reply: That is why Jewish people are still called and can be grafted back by faith. The calling is to Christ, not to territory.
attacks.rejoinder: Christian Zionists read the calling as including all the national promises.

attacks.attack: It makes Gentile Christians arrogant toward Jews.
attacks.reply: Paul forbids exactly that pride. The fulfilled reading, rightly held, calls Gentiles to humility, gratitude and longing for Israel's salvation.
attacks.distinction: Humility is part of the doctrine, not an add-on.
attacks.rejoinder: History shows the doctrine has often been held with pride.

attacks.attack: Revelation 7 lists the tribes, so ethnic Israel has a future role.
attacks.reply: John hears the number of the tribes, then sees a great multitude from every nation, as he heard of a lion and saw a lamb (5:5-6). The list is irregular: Dan is missing, Joseph and Manasseh both appear. It pictures the whole people of God as Israel's army.
attacks.distinction: John's hearing-then-seeing pattern joins the two groups.
attacks.rejoinder: Futurists see two distinct groups: a Jewish remnant sealed on earth and a Gentile multitude in heaven.

attacks.attack: Jesus said Jerusalem would see him again when it says “Blessed is he who comes.”
attacks.reply: The saying is conditional: Jerusalem would not see him until it welcomed him. It promises nothing about a state. Many fulfilled readers welcome a future turning of Jews to Christ.
attacks.distinction: A hope of conversion, not of restoration to the land.
attacks.rejoinder: Dispensationalists read it as a prophecy of national repentance at the return.

attacks.attack: “All Israel will be saved” proves a national future.
attacks.reply: Even if it means a future mass conversion, as many Reformed and postmillennial writers hold, it is salvation in Christ within the one olive tree, not a separate covenant or a land promise.
attacks.distinction: A future for Jewish people in Christ is part of fulfilment theology.
attacks.rejoinder: Dispensationalists link the salvation to the restored nation at Christ's return.

results.title: Kept in Christ
results.text: Follow the apostles' reading: the promise is kept in Christ and shared by all in him, Jew and Gentile.

results.title: Kept in Israel's history
results.text: The promise had its fulfilment before Christ; it does not point to modern events.

results.title: Weigh it carefully
results.text: Read the text in context with other Christians; be slow to tie it to the news, which has misled every generation.
